objectives: Distinguish B-tree vs LSM-tree storage engines.
Reason about read-heavy vs write-heavy workload fit.
Recognize the read amplification / write amplification / space amplification trade-offs.

slides.title: The two dominant storage-engine families
slides.body:
Two storage-engine families dominate modern databases, each with a decades-long lineage rooted in foundational research.

**B-trees** were invented by **Rudolf Bayer** and **Edward McCreight** at Boeing Research Labs in 1972. Their paper, "Organization and Maintenance of Large Ordered Indexes" (Acta Informatica, 1972), introduced a self-balancing tree structure in which every node is guaranteed to be between half-full and completely full — a property enforced by splits and merges on insert/delete. The **B+tree** variant, which stores all data in leaf nodes and uses internal nodes purely for routing, became the dominant form: every major relational engine — **PostgreSQL**, **MySQL InnoDB**, **Oracle**, **SQL Server**, **SQLite** — uses a B+tree for its primary storage.

The key B+tree properties:
- **Sorted on disk**: a range scan visits only leaf nodes in order — no random seeks.
- **In-place updates**: a write finds the correct leaf page, modifies it, and marks it dirty. The **write-ahead log (WAL)** records the change first, ensuring durability before the page is flushed.
- **Fill factor**: pages are kept at ~70-90% full by default, leaving room for inserts without immediate splits. Tunable per index.
- **Read cost**: $O(\log_b n)$ page reads for a point lookup in a tree of $n$ records with branching factor $b$.

**LSM-trees** (Log-Structured Merge-trees) emerged from the landmark paper **"The Log-Structured Merge-Tree (LSM-Tree)"** by **Patrick O'Neil, Edward Cheng, Dieter Gawlick, and Elizabeth O'Neil** (Acta Informatica, 1996). The central insight: random writes to spinning disk (and, later, to flash NAND) are far slower than sequential writes. LSM converts all writes to sequential I/O by first absorbing them into an in-memory buffer (the **memtable**), then flushing sorted immutable files (**SSTables** — Sorted String Tables) to disk. Background **compaction** periodically merges SSTables, discards deleted records, and re-sorts.

Major LSM-based systems:
- **Google Bigtable** (**Fay Chang, Jeffrey Dean, Sanjay Ghemawat**, et al., OSDI 2006) popularised SSTables at global scale.
- **LevelDB** (open-sourced by **Jeff Dean** and **Sanjay Ghemawat** at Google, 2011) is the canonical reference LSM implementation.
- **RocksDB** (Facebook, 2012, forked from LevelDB) added pluggable compaction strategies and became the embedded LSM engine of choice for **CockroachDB**, **Yugabyte**, **TiKV**, and **MyRocks**.
- **Apache Cassandra** (**Avinash Lakshman** and **Prashant Malik**, Facebook, 2008; open-sourced, Apache 2010) pairs LSM storage with a ring-based distributed architecture.
- **Amazon Dynamo** (**Giuseppe DeCandia, Deniz Hastorun, Madan Jampani**, et al., SOSP 2007) used a similar LSM + consistent-hashing approach and directly inspired Cassandra.

The choice is workload-dependent. Default assumption: B-tree unless you know writes dominate.

slides.title: Read / write / space amplification
slides.body:
Storage engine trade-offs are measured in three amplifications:

- **Write amplification (WA)**: how many bytes does the engine write to storage per byte of user data written? B-tree: ~1-3x (in-place update writes the modified page once, plus WAL). LSM: potentially 10-30x, because each byte travels through multiple compaction passes.
- **Read amplification (RA)**: bytes read from storage per byte of user data read. B-tree: $O(\log_b n)$ pages for a point lookup — typically 3-5 page reads for a large table. LSM: a key may live in the memtable, in an L0 SSTable, or in any deeper level; in the worst case the engine checks every level. **Bloom filters** (probabilistic data structures invented by **Burton Bloom** in 1970, "Space/Time Trade-offs in Hash Coding with Allowable Errors", CACM 1970) drastically reduce this by ruling out levels that definitely do not contain the key, keeping expected RA close to 1 for point lookups.
- **Space amplification (SA)**: actual disk used / logical data size. B-tree: ~1.3x (page fill factor leaves headroom). LSM: 1.1x to 10x depending on compaction strategy; stale versions of overwritten records pile up until compaction removes them.

**Compaction strategies** are the primary tuning lever in LSM engines:
- **Leveled compaction** (RocksDB default): each level $L_i$ is at most $T\times$ the size of $L_{i-1}$. A compaction merges one SSTable from $L_i$ with all overlapping SSTables in $L_{i+1}$. Reads are fast (at most one SSTable per level holds a given key); WA is $O(L \cdot T)$. With $L=7, T=10$: WA $\approx 70\times$.
- **Size-tiered compaction** (Cassandra default): when $k$ SSTables of similar size accumulate, they are merged into one larger SSTable. Lower WA but higher SA and slower reads.
- **FIFO compaction**: oldest SSTables are simply dropped; useful only for time-series data with TTL.

The **Bw-tree** (**Justin Levandoski**, David Lomet, Sudipta Sengupta, Microsoft Research, ICDE 2013) is a lock-free B-tree variant using a mapping table and delta records to avoid in-place writes, blending B-tree read characteristics with LSM-like write batching. It powers **Azure Cosmos DB**.

**WiscKey** (Lanyue Lu et al., FAST 2016) further refines LSM by separating keys (kept in the LSM tree) from values (appended to a separate value log), dramatically reducing WA for large-value workloads.

Real engines pick a point on the WA-RA-SA triangle. The right trade-off is workload-driven: high-write time-series prefers low WA; analytics with rare updates prefers low RA.

slides.title: Bloom filters, SSTables, and the full LSM write path
slides.body:
Understanding the end-to-end LSM write path reveals why the family dominates write-heavy benchmarks despite higher WA.

**The write path**:
1. A write arrives and is appended to the **write-ahead log (WAL)** on disk — sequential, fast, ensures durability.
2. The write is inserted into the in-memory **memtable** (usually a skip-list or red-black tree, sorted by key).
3. When the memtable reaches a size threshold (e.g., 64 MB in LevelDB), it is frozen and a new memtable takes writes. The frozen memtable is flushed to disk as an immutable **SSTable** at Level 0.
4. **Compaction** runs in the background, merging L0 SSTables into L1, L1 into L2, and so on, eliminating duplicate or tombstoned keys.

Every disk write in this path is sequential — the defining advantage over B-tree's random page writes.

**The read path** and **Bloom filters**:
A point lookup must check: memtable → L0 SSTables (possibly multiple, unordered) → L1 → … → L$_{max}$. Without optimization, this is $O(L)$ I/Os per lookup. **Bloom filters** — one per SSTable — answer "does this SSTable possibly contain key $k$?" in $O(1)$ with a tunable false-positive rate $\epsilon$. With $\epsilon = 1\%$ and $L=7$, expected I/Os per lookup drops to close to 1. The space cost: $\approx -\log_2(\epsilon) / \ln 2 \approx 9.6$ bits per key at $\epsilon=1\%$.

**B-tree read advantage**: because a B+tree is sorted and all leaves are linked, a range scan visits exactly the leaf pages in key order — no multi-level probing. LSM range scans must merge-sort iterators from all levels, which is why B-trees remain competitive for scan-heavy OLAP workloads.

**Operational differences**:
- **Compaction I/O**: RocksDB compaction can consume significant disk bandwidth; in production, it is common to rate-limit compaction (`rate_limiter` in RocksDB) to prevent it from starving foreground writes.
- **Tombstones**: LSM deletes are recorded as tombstone markers. Until compaction removes the tombstone and its target, deleted data occupies space. This is why LSM SA can spike during heavy delete workloads.
- **Read-modify-write on B-trees**: updating a field requires a read (fetch the page) + modify + write-back. On LSM, the application writes a new full record (or a delta, depending on implementation); the old version is cleaned up by compaction.

The **Amazon Dynamo** paper (DeCandia et al., SOSP 2007) demonstrated that an eventually-consistent, AP-oriented system built on LSM-like storage with **consistent hashing** and **vector clocks** could sustain millions of writes per second across datacenters — a scale impossible with traditional B-tree engines running on a single primary. **Apache Cassandra**, inheriting Dynamo's distribution model and LevelDB-style LSM storage, brought this pattern to the open-source world.

question.question: Your workload is sustained 50K writes/sec on a 10TB dataset, with reads ~10% of write rate. The right storage engine choice:
options: LSM-tree (RocksDB-based DB like CockroachDB or YugabyteDB) — better write throughput at this scale.
question.explanation: Sustained 50K writes/sec on 10TB strongly favors LSM. B-tree write amplification + lock contention on hot pages causes problems at this rate. Read amp can be managed with bloom filters. The CockroachDB / Yugabyte stack (RocksDB underneath) is purpose-built for write-heavy at scale.

hints: Compute the write throughput requirements: 50K * payload size.
B-tree's in-place writes have what failure mode at very high write rates?
slides.workedSolution: At 50K writes/sec sustained, B-tree's write contention becomes a problem: hot pages get locked + dirty + flushed repeatedly. LSM converts random writes to sequential (memory → sorted runs), absorbing burstiness. Compaction adds background work but doesn't block writes. The trade-off (LSM has more complex ops, occasionally worse read latency) is worth it at this scale.

question.question: Derive LSM write amplification
question.goal: LSM with $L$ levels, growth factor $T$ between levels (each level $L_i$ holds $T \times$ data of level $L_{i-1}$). Each datum is compacted up to $L$ times. Write amplification?

steps.prompt: Datum's journey: written to L_0, compacted to L_1, then to L_2, ..., then to L_{L-1}. Total writes per datum?
Each compaction merges $T$ levels' worth of data. So per byte written by user, total disk writes = ?
steps.reveal: Total writes per byte = $L \cdot T$. For RocksDB defaults ($L = 7, T = 10$): WA $\approx 70$. Adjustable via compaction strategy.

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{\text{LSM WA} \approx L \cdot T}$$ With $L$ levels + growth factor $T$, each byte gets written $\sim L \cdot T$ times. RocksDB defaults: WA ~70×. Modern variants (tiered compaction, leveled compaction with smaller T) tune this trade-off.

A team's data store choice
question.prompt: A startup serving a real-time feed of stock market events: ~100K writes/sec, simple key-value reads, sub-10ms query latency target. They're choosing between Postgres + a custom indexing layer vs RocksDB-based KV (e.g., FoundationDB). Walk through the trade-off in two sentences, including which they should pick + why.
Explain in two sentences why LSM-tree-based databases routinely dominate write-heavy benchmarks despite having higher write amplification than B-trees.
question.rubric: Mentions that LSM converts random writes to sequential disk I/O via memtable + sorted runs; sequential write throughput on SSD/NVMe is 10-100× higher than random; total bytes written matters less than the access pattern.
